h.en: Responsibilities of a Software Project Manager

body.en:
• Estimation and planning: project size, effort, cost and duration - then the task schedule that grows from it.
  • People choreography: pick team members, assign tasks to skills, review progress honestly.
  • Risk and change management: keep the risk register current; absorb requirement changes through a controlled process.
  • Communication hub: report status to management and customer; shield the team from daily interruptions.
  • Quality guard: insist reviews and tests actually happen - the schedule may flex, quality may not.
  • Mental model: the PM is the umbrella activities from Unit 1 embodied as one accountable person.

• The oldest metric: estimate how many lines the finished program will have (KLOC = thousands of lines), then effort follows from historical productivity data.
  • Strengths: intuitive, directly measurable against a delivered product.
  • Weaknesses: only computable AFTER coding; strongly language- and style-dependent (the same task is 40 LOC in Python, 200 in assembly); rewards verbosity and punishes reusable libraries.
  • Variant KLOC feeds COCOMO; variant function-independent FP (below) feeds early estimates.

• FP measures the functionality delivered, from the user's view, BEFORE code exists - directly from requirements/SRS.
  • Count five component types: external inputs, external outputs, external inquiries, internal logical files, external interface files - each at a simple/average/complex weight.
  • UFP = sum over components of (count × weight).
  • Adjust for product complexity: FP = UFP × [0.65 + 0.01 × ΣFi] over 14 influence factors (data communication, distribution, performance, reusability...), each rated 0-5.
  • Language-independent and estimable early - its scheduling superpower. Weakness: component weights carry some subjectivity and practice.

• Mini Bus-Booking app requirement: 2 input screens (route entry, booking entry), 1 output (receipt/PNR), 1 inquiry (seat availability), 1 internal file (bookings). All 'average'.
  • UFP = 2×4 + 1×5 + 1×4 + 1×10 = 8 + 5 + 4 + 10 = 27.
  • Suppose the 14 complexity factors sum to 30 (a typical medium project): FP = 27 × (0.65 + 0.01×30) = 27 × 0.95 ≈ 25.7 FP.
  • Using a calibration of ~5 FP per person-month in our environment → about 5.2 person-months of effort.
  • For your own project, count every screen, report, table and interface the same way - that count is your Practical 12 deliverable.

• COnstructive COst MOdel (Boehm, 1981): empirical equations turning estimated KLOC into effort, duration and team size.
  • Thre product classes: organic (small, familiar, relaxed constraints - a college app), semi-detached (mixed experience/limits), embedded (hard real-time, tight hardware, safety).
  • Basic COCOMO equations with class constants: E = a×(KLOC)b person-months; D = c×Ed months; N = E/D people.
  • Accuracy ladder: Basic (early, KLOC only) → Intermediate (multiplies by 15 cost drivers: personnel capability, product complexity...) → Detailed (drivers per phase, per subsystem).
  • COCOMO II modernises the same idea for reuse, prototyping and object points - syllabus says 'COCOMO / COCOMO II approach', so know both names.

• Estimate for our bus-booking app: judged organic, size about 10 KLOC.
  • Effort E = 2.4 × (10)1.05 ≈ 2.4 × 11.2 ≈ 27 person-months.
  • Duration D = 2.5 × (27)0.38 ≈ 2.5 × 3.5 ≈ 8.7 months.
  • Team size N = E / D ≈ 27 / 8.7 ≈ 3 people - matches a small class team with a lead.
  • Method rigour: always state (1) chosen class and WHY, (2) how KLOC was estimated, (3) the arithmetic, (4) the sanity check against FP results.

• Scheduling decomposes the project into tasks (a Work Breakdown Structure), estimates each task's effort, finds dependencies (testing waits on coding) and lays the tasks over a calendar with owners.
  • The work itself is a LOOP: list tasks → estimate → dependencies → draw chart → track weekly → re-plan - the schedule is rebuilt as fast as reality shifts (see flow chart).
  • Two charting styles follow from the chosen process model: Gantt for planned projects; sprint burndown for agile ones.

• One horizontal bar per task over weeks/months; bar length = duration; overlap = parallelism; a bar's end feeding the next bar's start shows dependencies.
  • Update bars with % done during reviews; slipping bars are impossible to hide - that visibility is the Gantt's power.
  • Strength: instantly readable by anyone, ideal for communicating plans; weakness: deep 'which delay kills the deadline?' (the critical path) needs annotations or a PERT-style companion.
  • Practical 14 (traditional track): host your project's tasks on an 8-week Gantt like the example.

• Track remaining effort daily through a sprint: the dashed ideal line drops evenly toward zero; the team's actual line above it = behind schedule, below it = ahead.
  • Set plotted points honestly each stand-up - the burndown answers "are we on time RIGHT NOW?" in one glance.
  • Compare: Gantt = when will everything happen; burndown = are we on time today. Sprint-based agile replaces per-task Gantts with per-sprint burndowns.
  • Practical 14 (agile track): plot remaining task-hours for your sprint every day and read the gap.

• A risk is an uncertain event that, if it happens, hurts the project (deadline, budget, quality, people).
  • Identification sources: checklists of classic software risks (team inexperience, changing requirements, unproven tech), brainstorming with the team, vendor/dependency review.
  • Assessment scores each risk by probability (P) and impact (I); risk exposure R = P × I ranks them - high/high demands action today, low/low just gets accepted.
  • Output: the risk register - risk description, P, I, R, owner, mitigation plan, trigger to watch.

• Mitigation strategies: avoid (drop the risky feature/tech), transfer (buy a proven library, outsource), reduce probability (prototype the scary part first - remember Spiral!), reduce impact (backups, extra buffer).
  • Only two roots work long-term: risk avoidance (design the risk out) and contingency (prepare a concrete plan B with a trigger).
  • Monitoring & control: re-scan risks weekly, watch trigger signs (API keeps changing, key developer's notice period), execute plan B when triggered, re-score the register.
  • Exam phrasing: the cycle identify → assess → mitigate → monitor repeats for the project's whole life - never a one-time activity.

q.en: List four responsibilities of a software project manager.

a.en: Estimation and planning, task/team assignment and tracking, risk and change management, stakeholder communication and quality guarding.

q.en: Why does a PM own risk management?

a.en: Risk scanning needs authority over schedule and budget - only the PM can act on the register.

q.en: What is project estimation?

a.en: Predicting size, effort, cost and duration before (and while) building - the basis of every plan.

q.en: Define LOC as a size metric.

a.en: Estimated or counted lines of code of the finished product (KLOC in thousands) - the oldest, simplest size unit.

q.en: Two weaknesses of LOC.

a.en: Available only after coding; language- and style-dependent, so it inflates verbose code and depresses reusable-library projects.

q.en: What is a Function Point?

a.en: A measure of functionality DELIVERED, counted from requirements (inputs, outputs, inquiries, files) - before any code exists.

q.en: List the five FP component types.

a.en: External inputs, external outputs, external inquiries, internal logical files, external interface files.

q.en: Write the FP adjustment formula.

a.en: FP = UFP x (0.65 + 0.01 x S Fi), with Fi the 14 general system characteristics scored 0-5.

q.en: Why is FP estimable earlier than LOC?

a.en: It is calculated from the SRS, i.e. before design and coding - perfect for planning in week 1.

q.en: Compute UFP: 2 inputs, 1 output, 1 inquiry, 1 internal file, all average.
What is COCOMO?

a.en: Boehm's empirical model converting estimated KLOC into effort, duration and team size via class-tuned constants.

q.en: Name COCOMO's three project classes.

a.en: Organic (small/familiar), semi-detached (mixed) and embedded (hard real-time/binding constraints).

q.en: Give the basic COCOMO effort and duration equations.

a.en: Effort E = a x (KLOC)^b person-months; Duration D = c x E^d months; team size N = E / D.

q.en: Organic constants for basic COCOMO?
Levels of COCOMO?

a.en: Basic (KLOC only), Intermediate (15 cost-driver multipliers), Detailed (drivers applied per phase).

q.en: Estimate E, D, N for an organic 10-KLOC app.
What is a Work Breakdown Structure?

a.en: The project decomposed hierarchically into tasks/subtasks - the input list for scheduling.

q.en: What is a task dependency?

a.en: A 'must finish before start' relation - testing depends on coding, deployment on testing.

q.en: What is a Gantt chart?

a.en: A bar chart: tasks listed vertically, calendar horizontally; bar length = duration; overlaps = parallel work.

q.en: Gantt strength and weakness?

a.en: Strength: instantly readable progress/schedule view. Weakness: critical-path and deep dependency effects hide unless annotated.

q.en: When is a flow chart used in scheduling?

a.en: To document the plan-building procedure itself: tasks -> estimate -> dependencies -> chart -> track -> re-plan.

q.en: What is a sprint burndown chart?

a.en: Daily plot of REMAINING sprint effort against an ideal straight line - shows instantly whether the team is ahead or behind.

q.en: Burndown above the ideal line means?

a.en: Behind schedule - more work remains than the plan expects today.

q.en: Which chart suits an agile team and why?

a.en: Burndown: one sprint scope, daily accuracy, zero drawing ceremony; a Gantt is redundant within a sprint.

q.en: Define risk in software projects.

a.en: An uncertain event which, if it occurs, harms the project - time, cost, quality or people.

q.en: Name three classic software risks.

a.en: Unrealistic schedule, changing requirements, key-person loss (also: unproven third-party tech).

q.en: Steps of risk management?

a.en: Identification, assessment (probability x impact), mitigation planning, monitoring and control.

q.en: What is risk exposure R?

a.en: R = probability x impact - the ranking number that decides which risks deserve attention.

q.en: High-probability high-impact risk - response?

a.en: Mitigate now: redesign it out, prototype early, add buffer - plus a concrete contingency (plan B).

q.en: What does risk monitoring do?

a.en: Re-scans the register weekly, watches triggers (vendor slipping, churning requirements) and fires plan B when triggered.

q.en: Avoid/transfer/reduce - examples?

a.en: Avoid: drop the risky feature. Transfer: buy a proven component. Reduce: prototype the unknown API first.

q.en: What is a risk register?

a.en: A living table: risk, probability, impact, R=P x I, owner, mitigation, trigger - one row per watched risk.

q.en: Why is Spiral called risk-driven? (link to U1)

a.en: Each cycle runs an explicit risk-analysis quadrant before more engineering spends.

q.en: Practical 12 deliverable?

a.en: Your project's FP count - table of the five components with weights, UFP, factor sum, final FP.

q.en: Practical 13 deliverable?

a.en: Basic COCOMO: chosen class with reason, estimated KLOC, E/D/N arithmetic.

q.en: Practical 14 deliverable?

a.en: Flow-chart the schedule steps; Gantt for a planned project or sprint burndown for an agile one.

q.en: Estimate effort if basic COCOMO says N = 4 for 8 months.

a.en: E = N x D = 32 person-months.

q.en: One sentence: estimation vs scheduling vs tracking.

a.en: Estimate predicts size/effort; scheduling turns it into a dated task plan; tracking measures reality against it.
